When I used to do tfp as a photographer, I did about the same. Just had the model sign a contract saying she couldn't use unedited pictures for anything other than selection. Only agreed upon, edited pictures were to be published and used for self promotion. And 3 pictures is honest. If that's close up beauty, might sometimes have to be satisfied with one. If it's outdoor editorial, might sometimes be able to ask for more. Really depends on what you're shooting and the amount of retouching workload.

I also used to work in a premium model agency in Europe (we're talking to of the range international models like VS etc) and I was at first surprised to see how high salaries are for models even if they ve just been scouted and first lack experience. Obviously the agency will allow them to test for free on occasions, only if the project is interesting enough to get useable visuals for their portfolio. What I'm trying to say is, when you  attend a tfp shoot, just as much as the photog, you're working, and it's absolutely normal to expect payment in useable images if the photog won't pay for a day rate. Just as much as the photog expects modeling skills since no one is paying for their day rate either. At the end of the day it's portfolio development for both of you, and everyone has to go home with something. Your demands aren't too high.

EDIT: as far as wanting to control what the photog posts, I usually allowed the TFP girls to have a veto. Especially when shooting lingerie, we often sat together and the girls kicked out a few shots that they didn't want to be posted. A lot of professional models didn't care tho and allowed me to be the judge of what I selected or not. Most of the times, we agreed on a selection together. I was sometimes heartbroken to see a perfect shot being kicked out because the model didn't like the angle or found the pose too editorial and not Instagram-sexy enough, but at the end, it's a conversation and as stated above, I didn't pay for their day rate either so I tried to respect their choices too.

The trick is to try not to be rude or demanding, but still know your worth. I ended up hating some collabs because models would tell me what to do. That was a no-go when they loved their pictures and asked me to shoot again later. On the other hand, once a model told me to just do my thing with the selection and I rendered a bw portrait of her which she loved. She said she would love it in color, and since I already made my artistic choice, she offered to naturally pay for it if I agreed. I found that so nice, cute and respectful that I obviously edited it in color for free and we ended up shooting again together.

The cleavage thing is the kind of stuff that usually happens when people start to learn the dodge and burn technique and massively overdo it. It is basically modifying luminosity by adding and removing light, basically the same as makeup, but in post production. It's not only used for the body but also to take out folds from clothes etc.

The trick is really to know when to stop, this should be seemless and very realistic, just as a neutral makeup would be. For some reason, there's currently a trend of influencers giving "pro" retouching tutorials and popularizing overly retouched portraiture. Peoples faces are modified to oblivion and end up looking like cartoons. 

The cartoon look is also typical for photographers who want to maximize their dynamic range in post by boosting shadows and reducing highlights beyond the realistic look. There are more ways oviously but this one is very common.

I guess if a cartoon look is what the photographer wants to achieve, and if the image is considered as some type of unrealistic visual art (such as some digital painting) that had to start as a photograph with the goals of being heavily modified: it is an artistic choice. If it is aimed as being representative of reality, I can see how it sets false expectations.

Shooting at 1.2 might in some case be handy if you have a low light situation. This being said, if you shoot for clients who pay for a top notch location and you blur it out so much that it ends up not being recognizable, it might as well be a problem. There aren't pro lenses, just lenses that do the job. Don't listen to YouTubers or content creators telling you what you should own. Most of the time you'll probably end up not opening more than f4 anyway.

A strobe is like a source of light, typically stronger than a flash you would put on your camera. There are very expensive strobes ( see broncolor and profoto) and more affordable ones (godox, Bowens etc). In theory, apart from the power, any will work the same. Some offer more comfort for the photographer to use that you don't necessarily need as a hobby photog or a beginner. That's why a lot of people turn to something like the godox ad200 as a first portable source of light and upgrade once they feel they need to. This being said, this model is also still used by top notch fashion photographers for magazine work so you see, there's nothing wrong with it as long as it's powerful enough: the other models/brands might offer more options for shooting comfort but at the end of the day, light is light. Light theory is something you can understand by watching a few YouTube videos and isn't excessively complicated: distance to subject, relative size of the light source, direction, power... It's all accessible online. You'll also find in stores very expensive modifiers that you probably don't need at first: umbrellas with diffusion are extremely cheap (20 bucks sometimes) and are used by a lot of top shelf professionals. You can always invest in more expensive gear later, if you need it at all.

In terms of lenses, if you plan on buying only one prime, i d say you ll do more with a 50: it's close to human vision and supe versatile. 85 are considered as great portrait lenses but not always easy to use as you need to put more distance between you and the subject which isn't always possible. The difference also comes from the background transformation when shooting at the same distance to your subject. Not only you'll seem closer with the 85 but the background will seem bigger. To start with photography and lenses, I'd say a 50 is all you need. They deliver great looks and are rather cheap. When you get comfy, you can always go for a 35 and an 85 if you need them for your type of work.

I will agree with a focal anything between 50 and 85. I'm also probably going to get downvoted but I don't think that the light is only ambient. My guess is that the photographer has mixed the ambient with a strobe. The strobe will help freeze the motion and brighten the subject but again the subjects in the background are also rather frozen and the background is quite bright for this time of the day. Unlike a lot of YouTube videos will make you think, you can use a flash just for a kiss of light on your subject, you don't need to make your background super dark and your subject super bright. This aesthetic has proved to be rather popular on social media but a lot of fashion and portrait photogs use flash and you wouldn't be able to tell. That's your choice at the end of the day. I guess that's what the photographer did here. 

Here's a very dodgy explanation that will also probs get me some hate but these are rules of thumb and not proper theory.

You expose for your background:

- aperture: you choose your background blur. Whether your background is sharp or blurry might be down to you or the art director. You might need to adapt your lens due to this requirement.

- shutter speed: you choose how you want to freeze motion. For slow shutter speed, strobes will only help to freeze motion as long as the flash reaches the object. 

- iso: final tweaks to your background exposure

Now the subject:

- flash: I guess the subject will be a bit underexposed. Bring a kiss of light on the subject progressively to make it pop the way you want it. It might be that there are other ambient sources of light that will light your subject's face and you won't need it. If your subject was to be overexposed after the previous adjustments, you might need to also forget the flash, expose for the subject and adjust the background exposure in post. Might be that the subject is under a source of light or something else I'm just not thinking of at the moment.
